displayQuote: Without music, life would be a mistake

meta.title: Who really said "Without music, life would be a mistake"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — genuinely Nietzsche. It's aphorism 33 of Twilight of the Idols (1889): “Ohne Musik wäre das Leben ein Irrtum.” The German and an early English translation are both public domain.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Without music, life would be a mistake'?
meta.ogDescription: A rare verified one: Nietzsche wrote it in Twilight of the Idols (1889), Maxims and Arrows 33 — usually quoted without its comic bagpipe context.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From ‘Maxims and Arrows’ (Sprüche und Pfeile), aphorism 33, in Twilight of the Idols (Götzen-Dämmerung, written 1888, published 1889). The German reads “Ohne Musik wäre das Leben ein Irrtum”; the exact English wording appears in Anthony M. Ludovici’s 1911 translation. This is a genuine, sourced line.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: What trifles constitute happiness! The sound of a bagpipe. Without music life would be a mistake. The German imagines even God as a songster.
trail: The German original — “Ohne Musik wäre das Leben ein Irrtum” — sits in Sprüche und Pfeile 33 of Götzen-Dämmerung, per Wikiquote’s sourced section, which attaches the German to the English.
The exact English wording “Without music life would be a mistake” is the middle sentence of aphorism 33 in Ludovici’s 1911 translation.
Nietzsche wrote Götzen-Dämmerung in 1888; it was published in 1889 — so both the German and Ludovici’s 1911 English are long in the public domain.
source.excerptNote: Aphorism 33 in full (Ludovici, 1911). The famous line is the middle sentence — the bagpipe and the singing God around it are usually dropped, along with the joke. German original: “Ohne Musik wäre das Leben ein Irrtum.”

sourceLink.text: Twilight of the Idols, Ludovici translation (Project Gutenberg)

source.rightsNote: The German text was first published in 1889 and Ludovici’s English translation in 1911 — both well before 1931, so the wording quoted here is in the public domain in the United States. (A modern copyrighted translation, e.g. Kaufmann or Hollingdale, would be a separate rights question, but the classic ‘a mistake’ wording predates those.)

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About the author
author.metaLine: 1844–1900 · German philosopher, philologist & critic of morality
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher whose late works — among them Twilight of the Idols (1889) — combined aphoristic wit with a sweeping critique of morality, religion and culture. A trained classical philologist and a serious lover of music (and one-time friend of Wagner), he returned again and again to music as a measure of life’s worth.

misattribution.heading: One correct name, two common distortions
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Nietzsche is right — unusually for a famous-name quote. The distortions are in the wording and the company it keeps.

items.why: Aphorism 33 is comic: “What trifles constitute happiness! The sound of a bagpipe. Without music life would be a mistake. The German imagines even God as a songster.” Quoted alone, the line reads as pure uplift; in place it’s a wry jab at what passes for happiness, per Ludovici’s 1911 text.
The German “Irrtum” is rendered as both “a mistake” and “an error” across translations; there is no single canonical English wording, so both are faithful.

items.scope: The spliced “God who could dance” version
items.why: It’s often padded to “…a mistake. I would only believe in a God who could dance.” That second sentence is Nietzsche too, but from a different book — Thus Spoke Zarathustra, ‘On Reading and Writing’ — not part of aphorism 33.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Nietzsche: Twilight of the Idols (1889), Maxims and Arrows 33 — verifiable in the sourced text, best read with its bagpipe and singing God intact.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Nietzsche put music at the centre of his philosophy from the start — The Birth of Tragedy (1872) argued that Greek tragedy was born from the spirit of music. By the time of Twilight of the Idols, written in a burst in 1888, he could compress that lifelong conviction into seven words.

The aphorism’s power is that it hides a serious claim inside a joke. The surrounding sentences mock cheap happiness and pious Germans; the music line lands as the one ‘trifle’ Nietzsche actually means.
detailsBody: Anthony M. Ludovici’s 1911 version, from which the standard English wording comes, titles the opening section ‘Maxims and Missiles’; later translators (Kaufmann, Hollingdale) use ‘Maxims and Arrows’ for the same Sprüche und Pfeile. The aphorism number, 33, is stable across editions.
